frenchCards.note: Source 'the bill' (la cuenta). The objective's 'the check' is the US variant of the same item and also maps here; no separate card.
The tip. If unsure, ask: Le pourboire est-il compris ? (France-typical variant: Le service est compris ?)
Payment card (la tarjeta). Carte bancaire on the card for clarity; when paying, par carte is enough, as in the Reader. La carte alone can also mean the menu.
The cash (el efectivo). En espèces = in cash. L'argent liquide is a common synonym.
The change you get back (el cambio). Not le change, which means currency exchange.
Generic 'the ice' (el hielo). La glace can also mean ice cream. For ice in a drink, French says des glaçons (ice cubes), as in the Reader.
The drinking straw. Source popote is a Mexican regional word; French has one standard term.
The cream (la crema), kept as cream. Not replaced by crème fraîche.

Complément pour francophones (séparé de la tâche source) : en anglais, « you » sert à la fois pour tu et pour vous ; la politesse passe par « Can you… ? », « Could you… ? » et « please ». Pour un ordre poli, dites en anglais : « Please bring me… », « Wait a moment, please. », « Keep the change. »

frenchVerbParadigms.explanation: Irregular with stem alternation (peux/peut/peuvent vs pouvons/pouvez), loosely parallel to Spanish puedo/podemos. Spanish usted puede maps to French vous pouvez, not il peut. Pouvez-vous...? = English 'Can you...?'; the conditional Pourriez-vous...? = English 'Could you...?'. Pouvoir has no imperative.

Regular -er verb, 'to bring'; the Spanish irregular yo form traigo has no French counterpart. Usted trae = vous apportez. The usted command tráigame = vous imperative Apportez-moi (English 'Please bring me...' with s'il vous plaît). Pronoun rule: m' before the verb in a question (Pouvez-vous m'apporter...?), but -moi after an affirmative imperative (Apportez-moi...).

Regular -er verb, 'to give'; Spanish irregular doy does not carry over. Usted da = vous donnez. In the lesson it appears as an infinitive after pouvoir: Pouvez-vous me donner un verre d'eau ? = 'Can you give me a glass of water?'. Vous imperative: Donnez-moi...

Spelling change y to i in the singular and ils forms (paie/paient); the variants je paye, ils payent also exist. Usted paga = vous payez; ¿Va a pagar...? = Vous allez payer...? Payer par carte / en espèces mirrors pagar con tarjeta / en efectivo (English: pay by card / in cash). Vous imperative: Payez.

Quedarse con (to keep) is reflexive in Spanish; French garder is a plain transitive -er verb. Usted se queda con = vous gardez. The formal usted command Quédese con el cambio = vous imperative Gardez la monnaie ('Keep the change.'). The other sense of quedarse, 'to stay', would be rester and is not used here.

internalDomainNotes: Setting kept as Oaxaca with Anna, Luis and 200 pesos; no euro conversion and no Lyon/France redesign.

Question vs imperative force now follows the source English line by line: Can you = Pouvez-vous (card 10, reader 1 and 3); Could you = Pourriez-vous (card 9, reader 5); commands = vous imperatives (cards 11-13, reader 4 and 8).
Card 10 and reader 1 are identical in the source and are now identical in French.
Gardez la monnaie is the primary rendering of 'Keep the change.'; Je vous laisse la monnaie is kept only as a note alternative, so the garder paradigm is used by the content.
Card 5 is generic la glace per instruction; the Reader uses contextual des glaçons for water with ice. Grading should accept 'ice' / 'the ice' for both.
Card 2 is la carte bancaire with a note; the Reader uses par carte, which is unambiguous when paying.

Modes: see (term) -> recall (Could-request) -> hear (Can-request) -> type (command, card 11) -> say (command, card 13) -> write (reader line, cash and 200 pesos). Every prompt contains the exact French source item and every target is the exact source English.
Answer acceptance: 'Could you bring me the check, please?' should be accepted as a US variant for card 9 / reader 5, since the source objective uses both 'bill' and 'check'.

Speaking output is English. The source speaking task is kept verbatim; the source objective's Spanish-specific 'usted commands' wording stays in sourceNotes only and is not presented as an English speaking objective. The learner-facing supplement glosses it as polite commands with please.

All five source verb slots are kept (poder, traer, dar, pagar, quedarse) with French mappings pouvoir, apporter, donner, payer, garder; each explanation states usted = vous and gives the relevant vous imperative.

Reader 0 keeps 'un café' for the venue so it maps to source English 'a café'; 'prend ... du café' covers the source's single verb for eggs and coffee. Cafétéria was avoided because it suggests a canteen.
residuals: Native French review still open, in particular: Gardez la monnaie (primary) vs Je vous laisse la monnaie (alternative); 'Gardez la monnaie comme pourboire' vs 'en pourboire'; 'un moment' vs 'un instant' on card 12.
Reader 0 repeats café in two senses (du café / un café). This was kept for fidelity to 'at a café' rather than adopting the critique's 'petit restaurant'; it needs a reviewer decision.
Card 'la glace' is ambiguous out of context (ice / ice cream) and differs from the Reader's 'des glaçons'; this follows the instruction and is noted on the card.
popote -> la paille: Mexican regional source term with no French regional counterpart; note only.
